title: A card worked in every SEPA country, but the cash still did not travel
explain:
A traveller used a bank card in five SEPA countries on one trip.

It worked everywhere.

Then the traveller tried to manage cash the same way across those countries, and found the rules changed at every border.

Here's how it happened:

→ Card used in any SEPA country, regardless of where it was issued
→ SEPA Cards Framework complete across the SEPA area
→ Visa and Mastercard as the two main card networks
→ Interoperability that was already working, accelerated by SEPA
→ Cash handling still different everywhere, the SEPA Cash initiative remains a work in progress

The assumption was:
"SEPA finished the job for cards and cash together."

Why?

The SEPA Cards Framework stands complete, and major projects that began in 2007 to 2010 are complete. But cash is a sensitive area and standardising practices everywhere in SEPA is a real challenge, so the SEPA Cash initiative is still ongoing.

Cards finished, cash still catching up.

BA Takeaway

When a programme claims SEPA coverage, ask which instrument it covers. A complete card framework says nothing about cash.

Keep these controls separate:

→ The SEPA Cards Framework, complete
→ The SEPA Cash initiative, ongoing
→ Card interoperability across countries
→ Cash practices, still different per country

The real requirement isn't "Are we SEPA compliant?"

It's "What evidence proves which SEPA instrument this covers?"

Have you seen a SEPA claim that covered cards but not cash?
takeaway: Cards finished, cash still catching up.

title: An MT103 for EUR 75,000 was sent to the wrong application, and the payment vanished from view
explain:
A bank sent an MT103 for EUR 75,000 to another bank.

It never arrived in the payment queue.

It had been sent through the General Purpose Application, which only carries system messages.

Here's how it happened:

→ Bank sends MT103 for EUR 75,000
→ Message routed through the General Purpose Application
→ GPA carries system messages only: a user writing to SWIFT, or SWIFT writing to a user
→ No user to user traffic is allowed on GPA
→ Payment never reaches the other bank's payment queue

The assumption was:
"SWIFT is SWIFT, any application will carry any message."

Why?

The FIN Application carries messages from one user to another, and alongside that it covers the user-to-user range MT1xx through MT9xx, the system messages MT0xx, plus other service messages such as acknowledgements. The distinction is about who a message can travel between, not the network itself.

The right network, the wrong application.

BA Takeaway

When a message goes missing, check the application it travelled on before checking the message itself. A user to user message on a system-only application never arrives.

Keep these controls separate:

→ The message and its type
→ The application it travels on
→ Who the message can travel between
→ The receiving queue it should land in

The real requirement isn't "Did we send the message?"

It's "What evidence proves it travelled on the application that carries user to user traffic?"

Have you seen a payment lost because it went through the wrong application?
takeaway: The right network, the wrong application.

title: A EUR 1,500 card payment was guaranteed, and the merchant asked who actually paid for that promise
explain:
A merchant accepted a EUR 1,500 card payment.

The customer later defaulted.

The merchant was still paid, because the issuer had guaranteed the payment.

Here's how it happened:

→ Customer pays EUR 1,500 by card
→ Issuer authorises the transaction after accepting all risk
→ Issuer guarantees payment to the merchant
→ Customer defaults
→ Merchant still paid, the issuer absorbs the loss

The assumption was:
"Interchange is a fee the card network charges."

Why?

Card networks do not charge interchange. The fee compensates the issuer, who takes on all the risk, authorises the transaction and guarantees payment to the merchant. That guarantee is what interchange pays for.

Interchange pays for the guarantee, not the network.

BA Takeaway

When a pricing discussion treats interchange as a network charge, correct it. The fee follows the risk, and the risk sits with the issuer.

Keep these controls separate:

→ The network, which does not charge interchange
→ The issuer, who takes the risk
→ The authorisation decision
→ The guarantee to the merchant

The real requirement isn't "What does the network charge?"

It's "What evidence proves who carries the risk on this transaction?"

Have you seen interchange blamed on the network when the issuer carries the risk?
takeaway: Interchange pays for the guarantee, not the network.

title: An AI agent paid a EUR 12,000 vendor invoice, and no human had authorised it
explain:
A vendor invoice for EUR 12,000 was paid on a Tuesday morning.

No human had approved the payment.

An AI agent had run its six steps and decided the invoice was fine.

Here's how it happened:

→ Agent understands the payment request
→ Agent verifies the payment details
→ Agent evaluates the payment
→ Agent authorises the payment itself
→ Agent executes the payment of EUR 12,000
→ Agent confirms the payment to the customer

The assumption was:
"If the agent follows the steps, the payment is safe."

Why?

The authorisation step is the control that makes the whole flow safe, and in this flow the agent authorised itself. Understand, verify and evaluate are checks. Authorise is the decision, and it cannot be the agent approving its own work.

An agent that authorises itself is not controlled, it is unsupervised.

BA Takeaway

When an AI agent pays, the authorisation must sit with a human or a separate control, with a limit, a named approver, and evidence of the approval. Execution without independent authorisation is not automation, it is exposure.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Understanding and verification
→ Evaluation
→ Independent authorisation
→ Execution and confirmation

The real requirement isn't "Can the agent pay the invoice?"

It's "What evidence proves a human approved this payment before it moved?"

Have you seen an automated payment go out with no independent approval?
takeaway: An agent that authorises itself is not controlled, it is unsupervised.

title: An AI agent spent EUR 8,000 on API calls in one weekend, a few cents at a time
explain:
An AI agent paid for API calls with stablecoins all weekend.

Each call cost a few cents.

By Monday morning the total was EUR 8,000, and no one had set a limit.

Here's how it happened:

→ Agent calls an API to do its work
→ Each call is paid instantly in stablecoins, pay per use
→ Micropayments flow with no human in the loop
→ Programmable payments trigger themselves
→ EUR 8,000 accumulates over the weekend, a few cents at a time

The assumption was:
"Small payments cannot add up to a big loss."

Why?

Internet-native payments let a machine pay a machine for exactly what it used, and that is the point. But pay per use with no cap, no daily limit and no alert turns a clever mechanism into an open tap. Micropayments are still payments.

A thousand tiny payments is still EUR 8,000.

BA Takeaway

When a machine pays a machine, the controls must be machine sized too: a spend cap, a velocity limit, an alert threshold, and a named owner who sees the total.

Keep these controls separate:

→ The payment mechanism
→ The spend cap
→ The velocity and alert limits
→ The owner who sees the total

The real requirement isn't "Can the agent pay per use?"

It's "What evidence proves the total spend stayed inside its limit?"

Have you seen micropayments add up to a loss no one noticed?
takeaway: A thousand tiny payments is still EUR 8,000.

title: An AI assistant drafted a BRD in minutes, and the EUR 100,000 settlement leg was missing
explain:
A bank asked an AI assistant built for banking to draft a business requirements document for a new payment flow.

The BRD arrived in minutes, and it looked complete.

The settlement leg for EUR 100,000 was missing from it entirely.

Here's how it happened:

→ AI assistant drafts the BRD from banking knowledge
→ Customer conversation flows and requirements captured
→ Document reads well and is approved quickly
→ Build starts on the BRD
→ Settlement leg discovered missing during testing, EUR 100,000 with nowhere to settle

The assumption was:
"An assistant built for banking understands banking."

Why?

The assistant is aimed at the daily work of a banking professional, and it can draft fast. But a BRD is not a summary of banking knowledge. It is a complete statement of one specific flow, and only a person who owns that flow can say whether a leg is missing.

Fast drafting is not complete requirements.

BA Takeaway

An AI-drafted BRD still needs a human owner to walk the full payment journey, message by message, and sign that every leg is in it. Speed is a benefit only after completeness is proved.

Keep these controls separate:

→ The AI draft
→ The human walkthrough of the full journey
→ The settlement leg, named explicitly
→ The sign-off that the BRD is complete

The real requirement isn't "Can the assistant draft the BRD?"

It's "What evidence proves every leg of the payment is in the document?"

Have you seen an AI-drafted document approved before anyone checked it was complete?
takeaway: Fast drafting is not complete requirements.

title: A BRD promised in ten minutes took three days to fix, and the payment was late
explain:
A banking chatbot and BRD tool promised the same document in ten minutes instead of three days.

The team took the ten-minute BRD and started building.

Three days later they were still fixing it, and the payment flow went live late.

Here's how it happened:

→ Tool promises a BRD in ten minutes
→ Document delivered fast, same shape as the old three-day version
→ Build starts immediately
→ Gaps found in the payment logic during build
→ Three days spent fixing the document the tool had produced in ten minutes

The assumption was:
"Faster means better."

Why?

The claim is about speed: the same banking document, produced far faster. But a document produced fast and then fixed for three days is not faster. The time moved from drafting to rework, and the payment still went live late.

Ten minutes to draft, three days to fix, is not ten minutes.

BA Takeaway

Measure a tool by the time from request to a correct document, not from request to a first draft. Rework time counts.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Drafting time
→ Review and rework time
→ The payment logic, verified end to end
→ The go-live date, protected

The real requirement isn't "How fast can the document be produced?"

It's "What evidence proves the document was right the first time?"

Have you seen a fast draft cost more time in rework than the slow version would have?
takeaway: Ten minutes to draft, three days to fix, is not ten minutes.

title: A EUR 60,000 payment vanished between states, and no one could say which state it was in
explain:
A customer sent a EUR 60,000 payment.

It never arrived.

Operations searched for it, but no one could say which state it was in, because no state had a named owner or a piece of evidence.

Here's how it happened:

→ Initiation creates the instruction with an instruction ID and an end-to-end ID
→ Validation checks the instruction
→ Routing chooses the rail
→ Clearing moves it through the scheme
→ Settlement moves the funds between banks
→ Posting records it in the ledger
→ Confirmation tells the customer it is done
→ The payment stopped somewhere in the chain, and the evidence stopped with it

The assumption was:
"The payment will be found by asking around."

Why?

A payment moves through a chain of states from initiation to confirmation, and each state needs a named owner and a named piece of evidence. When a payment goes missing, the investigation follows this chain state by state, because the state where the evidence stops is the state where the payment is stuck.

The state where the evidence stops is where the payment is stuck.

BA Takeaway

Give every state an owner and an evidence item before the first payment flows. When one goes missing, walk the chain state by state and stop where the evidence stops.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Initiation and its IDs
→ Validation, routing, clearing
→ Settlement and posting
→ Confirmation to the customer
→ The owner and evidence for each state

The real requirement isn't "Where is the payment?"

It's "What evidence proves which state it reached?"

Have you seen a payment vanish because no state had an owner?
takeaway: The state where the evidence stops is where the payment is stuck.

title: A EUR 2,500 card payment was declined at authorisation, and the team investigated settlement
explain:
A customer tried to pay EUR 2,500 by card.

The payment was declined at the terminal.

The team spent a day investigating settlement, because no one had named which stage the failure belonged to.

Here's how it happened:

→ Terminal sends card and transaction details to the acquirer
→ Scheme routes them to the issuer
→ Issuer checks card status, available credit and fraud rules
→ Issuer declines and places no hold on the funds
→ Team investigates clearing and settlement, the wrong stages
→ The failure was at authorisation, in seconds

The assumption was:
"A card failure is a card failure, any stage will do."

Why?

A credit card transaction has four distinct stages with different owners and different evidence. Authorisation happens in seconds, clearing exchanges the transaction records, settlement moves the funds between the banks, and billing and dispute touchpoints handle the customer statement and any later dispute. Each stage must be understood separately, because a problem at authorisation looks nothing like a problem at settlement.

The wrong stage means the wrong investigation.

BA Takeaway

When a card payment fails, name the stage first: authorisation, clearing, settlement, or billing and disputes. Then investigate that stage, with its owner and its evidence.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Authorisation, in seconds
→ Clearing, exchanging records
→ Settlement, moving funds
→ Billing and disputes, handling the statement

The real requirement isn't "Why did the card payment fail?"

It's "What evidence proves which stage it failed at?"

Have you seen a team investigate the wrong stage of a card payment?
takeaway: The wrong stage means the wrong investigation.

title: pacs.008 passed the clearing system. Where is the pacs.002?
explain:
A EUR 75,000 payment is sent through the clearing system to the beneficiary bank.
The pacs.008 has gone.
The beneficiary bank is waiting, the customer is asking, and nobody can say where the status reply is.

Here's how that happens:

→ pacs.008 sent to the clearing system
→ Clearing system processes the payment
→ pacs.008 reaches the beneficiary bank
→ pacs.002 status reply travels back through the clearing system

The assumption was:
"The clearing system is just a pipe."

The clearing system sits between the originator bank and the beneficiary bank, so the pacs.008 passes through it and the pacs.002 returns through it. An analyst drawing the flow must include the clearing system as a party, not as a pipe, because it sends and receives messages of its own.

The clearing system is a party, not a pipe.

BA Takeaway

Draw the clearing system as a party with messages of its own. The pacs.008 passes through it on the way out, and the pacs.002 passes through it on the way back, and each hop is a message with a sender, a receiver and a status.

Keep these controls separate:

→ pacs.008 outward
→ Clearing system processing
→ pacs.008 to beneficiary bank
→ pacs.002 status back

The real requirement isn't "Did the payment leave?"

It's "What evidence proves where the pacs.008 is, and where the pacs.002 reply stands?"

Have you ever drawn a payment flow and left the clearing system out as if it were just a wire?
takeaway: An analyst drawing the flow must include the clearing system as a party, not as a pipe, because it sends and receives messages of its own.

title: The MT103 in a language nobody at the bank speaks
explain:
A EUR 15,000 payment is sent to a beneficiary bank in a country whose language is not English.
The names and addresses in the message are in the local language.
The operations team stares at the MT103 and wonders whether it can even be processed.

Here's how that happens:

→ MT103 arrives with names in the local language
→ Structured fields carry the account, currency and amount
→ Processing follows the coded fields

The assumption was:
"The message must be in English to be processed."

When the beneficiary bank is in a country whose language is not English, the MT103 is still processed from its structured fields, which are coded and do not depend on the language of the country. The names and addresses in the message may be in the local language, but the fields that drive processing, such as the account number, the currency, and the amount, are numeric or coded. Processing therefore does not stop at a language barrier; it follows the fields.

Processing follows the fields, not the language.

BA Takeaway

Read the coded fields, not the alphabet. Account number, currency and amount are numeric or coded, and they drive processing whatever language the names are written in.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Structured fields are coded
→ Names may be in the local language
→ Account, currency and amount drive processing

The real requirement isn't "Can we read the names?"

It's "What evidence proves the coded fields are complete and valid?"

Have you ever held a payment because the names were in a language nobody on the team could read?
takeaway: Processing therefore does not stop at a language barrier; it follows the fields.

title: Faster Payments is not SEPA with a different name
explain:
A team that knows SEPA is asked to build the flow for UK Faster Payments and BACS.
They reach for the SEPA messages, because the concepts look the same: initiation, clearing, status reporting.
Then the first GBP 25,000 payment fails, because the UK messages are not the SEPA messages.

Here's how that happens:

→ SEPA concepts: initiation, clearing, status
→ UK Faster Payments messages differ from SEPA
→ BACS messages differ from SEPA
→ Payment fails on the wrong message set

The assumption was:
"SEPA messages work everywhere."

The messages exchanged between banks in UK Faster Payments and in BACS are different from the messages used in SEPA. The SEPA message set is a good starting point, because the concepts of initiation, clearing, and status reporting are the same, but the actual messages and the clearing systems differ. An analyst who understands the SEPA flow can learn the UK flows by mapping each SEPA message to its UK equivalent, rather than starting from nothing.

Same concepts, different messages. Map, do not assume.

BA Takeaway

Use SEPA as the starting point, then map each SEPA message to its UK equivalent. Initiation, clearing and status reporting work the same way, but the actual messages and the clearing systems differ, and the mapping is the work.

Keep these controls separate:

→ SEPA initiation message
→ UK Faster Payments equivalent
→ BACS equivalent
→ Clearing system per rail

The real requirement isn't "Do we know SEPA?"

It's "What evidence proves each SEPA message has a named UK equivalent?"

Have you ever assumed one message set worked on another rail and watched the payment fail?
takeaway: An analyst who understands the SEPA flow can learn the UK flows by mapping each SEPA message to its UK equivalent, rather than starting from nothing.

title: Faster Payments settles in seconds. Salaries still run on BACS.
explain:
Faster Payments settles a payment in seconds.
Yet every month, a business with 2,000 employees pays salaries through BACS, a system older than most of its staff.
The faster rail is there, and the business still chooses the slower one.

Here's how that happens:

→ Faster Payments settles single payments in seconds
→ Business pays 2,000 salaries through BACS
→ Bulk run arrives on schedule, at low cost

The assumption was:
"Faster makes BACS obsolete."

Faster Payments is built for single, urgent payments, and it costs more per payment and carries limits that bulk runs do not want. BACS is built for bulk, scheduled, low-cost payments such as salaries and supplier runs. The two systems therefore serve different needs, and the older one survives because it fits the bulk use case better.

The older rail survives because it fits the bulk use case.

BA Takeaway

Match the rail to the use case, not to the speed. Single and urgent goes Faster Payments. Bulk, scheduled and low-cost goes BACS, and the salary run is the textbook bulk case.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Single urgent payments
→ Bulk scheduled payments
→ Cost per payment
→ Limits per payment

The real requirement isn't "Which rail is faster?"

It's "What evidence proves this rail fits this use case on cost, limits and timing?"

Have you ever recommended the fastest rail for a job the oldest rail does better?
takeaway: The two systems therefore serve different needs, and the older one survives because it fits the bulk use case better.

title: The MT103 says euros. The MT202 COV says dollars.
explain:
A cover payment is sent, and the two legs carry different currencies.
The MT103 says euros. The MT202 COV says dollars.
The operations team assumes one of them is wrong, and holds the EUR 150,000 payment.

Here's how that happens:

→ MT103 instruction in euros
→ MT202 COV in dollars
→ Fields 52, 53 and 54 describe the chain
→ Payment held while the mismatch is investigated

The assumption was:
"Both legs must carry the same currency."

In a cover payment the MT103 and the MT202 can carry different currencies, and the question is how the currency of each leg is decided and what fields 52, 53 and 54 carry. Field 52 identifies the ordering institution, field 53 identifies the sender's correspondent, and field 54 identifies the receiver's correspondent, so together they describe the chain of banks that will fund the payment. The currency of the cover leg follows the correspondent account it settles in, which is why the two legs can differ.

The cover currency follows the correspondent account it settles in.

BA Takeaway

Read fields 52, 53 and 54 before calling a mismatch. They name the ordering institution, the sender's correspondent and the receiver's correspondent, and the cover currency follows the correspondent account it settles in.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Field 52, ordering institution
→ Field 53, sender's correspondent
→ Field 54, receiver's correspondent
→ Cover currency follows its account

The real requirement isn't "Do the two legs match?"

It's "What evidence proves each leg's currency follows the account it settles in?"

Have you ever held a cover payment because the two legs showed different currencies?
takeaway: The currency of the cover leg follows the correspondent account it settles in, which is why the two legs can differ.

title: A future-dated MT103 for EUR 200,000, offered as security
explain:
An MT103 value-dated far in the future is presented to a bank, and the holder asks the bank to discount it.
EUR 200,000, dated months ahead, offered as if it were money already promised.
The bank declines, and the holder cannot understand why a payment instruction is not a promise.

Here's how that happens:

→ MT103 value-dated far in the future
→ Presented to the bank for discounting
→ MT103 is an instruction to pay
→ Payer account holds sufficient funds, or it does not

The assumption was:
"A future MT103 is proof the money will arrive."

An MT103 is an instruction to pay, not a proof of financial commitment: when the due date arrives, execution depends on the payer account holding sufficient funds. If the payer does not pay, the beneficiary has no recourse, and neither does a bank that discounted it, unless it signed a separate contract with the payer.

An MT103 is an instruction to pay, not proof of financial commitment.

BA Takeaway

Never treat an MT103 as security. At the due date the payment executes only if the payer's account holds sufficient funds, and without a separate contract with the payer, a discounting bank has no recourse.

Keep these controls separate:

→ MT103 as instruction
→ Payer funds at the due date
→ Beneficiary recourse
→ Separate contract with the payer

The real requirement isn't "Is the MT103 genuine?"

It's "What evidence proves the payer is committed to pay, beyond the instruction itself?"

Have you ever been offered a future-dated MT103 as if it were a guarantee?
takeaway: If the payer does not pay, the beneficiary has no recourse, and neither does a bank that discounted it, unless it signed a separate contract with the payer.

title: France before SEPA: PNS, TBF, then CORE
explain:
Before SEPA, France already ran EBA systems for interbank payments alongside high value systems called PNS and TBF.
Then SEPA arrived, and CORE, the retail clearing system, came after it to process XML format files.
Old systems, new systems, and a market that changed underneath them, with a EUR 2 million retail file caught in the middle of the changeover.

Here's how that happens:

→ PNS and TBF run high value payments
→ EBA systems handle interbank payments
→ SEPA arrives, market infrastructures change
→ CORE arrives after SEPA for retail

The assumption was:
"SEPA replaced everything overnight."

The market infrastructures changed greatly with the SEPA project, with old and new systems sitting side by side for a time. CORE, the retail clearing system, arrived after SEPA to process XML format files and improve retail payment services.

Old and new systems sat side by side while the market changed.

BA Takeaway

Map the changeover as a timeline, not a switch. PNS and TBF ran high value, EBA systems ran interbank, and CORE arrived after SEPA for retail, with old and new sitting side by side.

Keep these controls separate:

→ PNS and TBF, high value
→ EBA systems for interbank
→ CORE for retail
→ Old and new side by side

The real requirement isn't "Which system do we use now?"

It's "What evidence proves which system carried each payment during the changeover?"

Have you ever had to explain why two systems ran side by side for the same kind of payment?

title: RuPay: the scheme that is also the clearing house
explain:
A RuPay card payment of Rs 12,000 is made between two RuPay member banks.
The issuer expects the transaction to clear through a separate clearing house.
It does not. The scheme clears it itself.

Here's how that happens:

→ Issuer and acquirer are both RuPay members
→ Transaction clears through RuPay itself
→ NPCI operates RuPay in India

The assumption was:
"A scheme always needs a separate clearing house."

On RuPay, clearing and settlement run between domestic and other network partners, with RuPay acting as both the card scheme and the clearing house. In India the clearing house role sits with NPCI, which operates RuPay. When issuer and acquirer are both RuPay members, they clear their transactions through RuPay itself rather than through a separate clearing house.

Two RuPay members clear through RuPay itself.

BA Takeaway

Check membership before assuming a separate clearing house. When issuer and acquirer are both RuPay members, clearing and settlement run through RuPay itself, operated by NPCI.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Scheme role
→ Clearing house role
→ NPCI as operator
→ Member to member clearing

The real requirement isn't "Which clearing house cleared it?"

It's "What evidence proves both banks are RuPay members, and that RuPay cleared it?"

Have you ever looked for a separate clearing house behind a payment the scheme cleared itself?

title: Who sends the pacs.002? It depends on the rail.
explain:
A EUR 30,000 payment is sent, and the status reply never arrives.
The team waits for the beneficiary bank to answer.
On this rail, the beneficiary bank was never the one who answers.

Here's how that happens:

→ Payment sent
→ Status reply expected
→ Wrong party waited on
→ Reply already sent by the clearing mechanism

The assumption was:
"The beneficiary bank always sends the status."

The sender of a status response depends on the rail the payment travelled. On a real time gross settlement system the clearing and settlement mechanism sends pacs.002, pacs.004 and camt.029 to the originator. On a cross-border payment the beneficiary bank, or instructed bank, sends them.

On RTGS the clearing mechanism answers. Abroad, the beneficiary bank does.

BA Takeaway

Check the rail before waiting on a reply. On RTGS the clearing and settlement mechanism sends pacs.002, pacs.004 and camt.029 to the originator. On a cross-border payment the beneficiary bank, or instructed bank, sends them.

Keep these controls separate:

→ RTGS, the CSM answers
→ Cross-border, the beneficiary bank answers
→ pacs.002, pacs.004, camt.029

The real requirement isn't "Who do we usually wait for?"

It's "What evidence proves which party sends the status on this rail?"

Have you ever waited for a status reply from a bank that was never going to send it?
takeaway: On a cross-border payment the beneficiary bank, or instructed bank, sends them.

title: Cycle 00 arrived. The indirect participant got nothing.
explain:
A direct participant signs up for scheme cycle 00.
The cycle 00 transactions arrive, and the direct participant receives them all.
The indirect participant, who never signed up, receives nothing, and its customers wait for payments that were never forwarded.

Here's how that happens:

→ Direct participant signs up for cycle 00
→ Cycle 00 transactions arrive
→ Indirect participant did not enrol
→ Nothing forwarded to the indirect participant

The assumption was:
"Signing up covers everyone downstream."

Cycle sign-up belongs to the direct participant alone, so a direct participant enrolled for cycle 00 receives those transactions yet sends nothing to an indirect participant that did not enrol. Forwarding runs on a timetable the two agree separately, for instance once at the end of the day, and stays independent of the cycles. In classic SEPA only the direct participant exchanges files with the clearing and settlement mechanism. In SCT Inst some indirect participants connect directly to the mechanism and files move immediately, so no cycles exist there.

A direct participant enrolled for cycle 00 receives those transactions yet sends nothing to an indirect participant that did not enrol.

BA Takeaway

Sign up each participant, and agree forwarding separately. Cycle sign-up belongs to the direct participant alone, forwarding runs on a timetable the two agree, and in SCT Inst some indirect participants connect directly, so no cycles exist there.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Cycle sign-up, direct participant only
→ Forwarding, separately agreed
→ Classic SEPA, direct participant only
→ SCT Inst, direct indirect links

The real requirement isn't "Did we sign up for the cycle?"

It's "What evidence proves the indirect participant is enrolled, or will be forwarded to?"

Have you ever watched a cycle arrive in full while a downstream participant received nothing?

title: Two fields in pacs.008 tell you who really paid
explain:
A EUR 28,000 pacs.008 arrives, and the operations team cannot tell whether the payer was a direct participant or an indirect one.
The answer is in the message, in two fields they never thought to read together.

Here's how that happens:

→ pacs.008 arrives
→ Instructing agent named
→ Debtor agent named
→ Participation model revealed

The assumption was:
"The debtor agent is always the payer."

Two agents in pacs.008 reveal the participation model behind a payment. Where the payer is a direct participant, both instructing agent and debtor agent name that direct participant. Where the payer is indirect, the instructing agent still names the direct participant while the debtor agent names the indirect participant.

Two fields tell the story. Read them together.

BA Takeaway

Read instructing agent and debtor agent together. Direct payer: both name the direct participant. Indirect payer: the instructing agent still names the direct participant, while the debtor agent names the indirect participant.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Instructing agent
→ Debtor agent
→ Direct payer pattern
→ Indirect payer pattern

The real requirement isn't "Who sent the message?"

It's "What evidence proves who really paid, the instructing agent or the debtor agent?"

Have you ever read one agent field and assumed you knew who paid?
takeaway: Where the payer is indirect, the instructing agent still names the direct participant while the debtor agent names the indirect participant.

title: TAG 21 never leaves the MT101
explain:
A corporate customer sends an MT101 for EUR 18,000, with TAG 21 filled in for its own reporting.
The MT103 that follows carries no TAG 21.
The customer calls to ask where their reference went, and the operations team cannot explain why it stopped.

Here's how that happens:

→ MT101 received with TAG 21
→ MT103 generated without TAG 21
→ Customer asks where the reference went

The assumption was:
"Every field travels forward."

TAG 21 of an MT101 never maps into the MT103 that follows. It serves reporting to the ordering customer about the MT101, letting that customer reconcile the reporting automatically with the original transaction. TAG 21 stops there and never travels to the next party in the chain.

TAG 21 stops there and never travels to the next party in the chain.

BA Takeaway

Tell the customer up front: TAG 21 is for reporting to the ordering customer, so they can reconcile the reporting with the original transaction. It never maps into the MT103, and it never travels to the next party in the chain.

Keep these controls separate:

→ TAG 21 in the MT101
→ Customer reporting
→ Reconciliation with the original transaction
→ MT103 without TAG 21

The real requirement isn't "Did the MT103 carry everything?"

It's "What evidence proves the customer knows which fields travel forward and which stop?"

Have you ever had a customer chase a reference that was never meant to travel beyond their own report?

title: E-mandates need a router. It does not have to be a CSM.
explain:
A creditor bank needs to route e-mandate messages to debtor banks across the SEPA area.
The team assumes only a clearing and settlement mechanism can do it.
The mandate for EUR 2,000 a month waits while they look for a CSM to hire.

Here's how that happens:

→ Creditor bank needs e-mandate routing
→ No CSM in the middle
→ Mandates wait for a router

The assumption was:
"Only a clearing system can route e-mandates."

A creditor bank needs a player in between to route e-mandate messages to debtor banks, but that player does not have to be a clearing and settlement mechanism. The operating model defines two services for this: routing and validation, each delivered by a service provider, and either service can come from a debtor bank, a creditor bank or a CSM. Market players provide this kind of routing service, and a search for SEPA e-mandate providers finds more names.

The operating model defines two services, routing and validation, and either can come from a debtor bank, a creditor bank or a CSM.

BA Takeaway

Buy the two services, not a clearing system. Routing and validation are each delivered by a service provider, and either one can come from a debtor bank, a creditor bank or a CSM.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Routing service
→ Validation service
→ Service provider options
→ Debtor bank, creditor bank or CSM

The real requirement isn't "Which CSM do we use?"

It's "What evidence proves the routing and validation services are covered, whoever provides them?"

Have you ever assumed only a clearing system could do a job any service provider could do?

explain:
The monthly salary file went to BACS a day late.
Payday moved a day.
No one could hurry it back.

Here is how that happens:

→ Salary file submitted one day late
→ Day one for submission becomes day two
→ Day two for processing becomes day three
→ Day three for settlement becomes day four
→ Salaries land a day after payday

The assumption said:
"BACS is electronic. It can be hurried."

So the file missed its submission day and the team discovered that the three-day cycle is a rule, not a suggestion.

Why?

BACS takes three working days: day one for submission, day two for processing, and day three for settlement. BACS is built for bulk, scheduled, low-cost payments such as salaries and supplier runs, and that is why it outlasts Faster Payments for bulk pay. Faster Payments is built for single, urgent payments, and it costs more per payment and carries limits that bulk runs do not want.

BACS does not hurry. The calendar is the control.

A day late at submission is a day late at payday, every time.

BA Takeaway

A BACS file is a three-day promise. Submit it on day one or move payday.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Submission day, fixed in the payroll calendar
→ Processing day, owned by the file team
→ Settlement day, the payday everyone sees
→ Fallback plan when a file misses its day

The real requirement is not "Can we send the salaries today?"

It is "What evidence proves the file was submitted in time for payday?"

Have you seen a payday move because a BACS file missed its day?
takeaway: BACS does not hurry. A BACS file is a three-day promise, submit it on day one or move payday.

explain:
A supplier invoice for EUR 50,000 was due on Friday. The payment team sent it serial, straight down the chain, and marked the job done.

On Monday the supplier had still not been paid. The money was sitting with an intermediary bank, going nowhere.

Here is what happened:

→ MT103 sent serial to the first intermediary
→ Intermediary deducts its charge and passes it on
→ Next bank has no account relationship with the beneficiary bank
→ MT103 returned, funds parked, supplier unpaid

The requirement said:
"Send every MT103 serial unless told otherwise."

So nobody checked whether the route could actually settle.

Why?

A serial payment only works where each bank in the chain holds an account with the next bank. The sending bank held no account with the beneficiary bank, so the correct route was a cover payment: an MT103 sent direct to the beneficiary bank, and an MT202 COV settling the funds through the correspondent that held the dollars.

Serial is a chain of accounts. No account, no chain.

The method has to be chosen from the account relationships, not from habit. Check the relationships first, then pick serial or cover.

BA Takeaway

The payment method is a design decision, not a default.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Account relationships on the route
→ Method selection, serial or cover
→ Intermediary count and charges

The real requirement is not "Which method do we usually use?"

It is "What evidence proves this route can settle before we send?"

Have you ever watched a payment bounce between intermediaries because nobody checked the route first?

explain:
A customer sent USD 25,000 to pay an invoice and was told the payment had gone. Three days later the beneficiary called to say nothing had arrived.

The payment had gone. The money had not.

Here is what happened:

→ MT103 sent to the beneficiary bank
→ MT202 COV still travelling through the cover chain
→ Beneficiary bank holds the instruction and waits
→ Customer told "payment sent" on the MT103 date
→ Beneficiary unpaid until the cover settles

The requirement said:
"Confirm the payment as sent when the MT103 leaves."

So the customer was told the job was done while the funds were still in transit.

Why?

In a cover payment the MT103 and the MT202 COV travel separately, so the MT103 can reach the beneficiary bank before the funds leg arrives. The beneficiary bank must hold the instruction and wait for the cover, because it cannot credit the beneficiary until the funds have settled. This timing gap is a normal feature of the cover method, not an error.

Sent is not settled. The MT103 is the message, the cover is the money.

The gap is also the moment when an amount or reference mismatch is most likely to surface, so the wait is doing real work.

BA Takeaway

Instruction sent and funds settled are two different events.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Instruction status
→ Cover funds status
→ Beneficiary credit status

The real requirement is not "When did the MT103 leave?"

It is "What evidence proves the funds have settled before we tell the customer it is done?"

Have you ever had to explain to a customer that "sent" did not mean "received"?
takeaway: Sent is not settled. The MT103 is the message, the cover is the money.

explain:
A company paid an overseas employee EUR 5,000 in salary by MT103. The employee received EUR 4,940 and asked where the missing EUR 60 had gone.

Nobody had made an error. The payment had simply passed through two intermediary banks.

Here is what happened:

→ MT103 sent for EUR 5,000
→ First intermediary deducts EUR 35
→ Second intermediary deducts EUR 25
→ Beneficiary bank credits EUR 4,940
→ Employee asks why the salary is short

The requirement said:
"The amount sent is the amount the beneficiary receives."

So nobody warned the employee, and nobody priced the route.

Why?

In a serial payment the ordering customer bears the charges, and each intermediary bank deducts its own charge from the amount as the payment passes through. The beneficiary therefore receives the amount minus the charges deducted at each step. The shortfall is the charge, not an error, and it is why the charge-bearer matters before the payment is sent.

In a serial payment, every bank in the chain takes its cut from the amount.

Field 71A states who bears the charges, and field 71F states the amount of each charge deducted, so the final credit can be reconciled against the amount the ordering customer sent.

BA Takeaway

Price the whole chain, not just the first step.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Charge bearer in field 71A
→ Each deduction in field 71F
→ Beneficiary communication before the payment

The real requirement is not "Did we send EUR 5,000?"

It is "What evidence proves the beneficiary will receive the amount we promised?"

Have you ever had to explain a short salary to an employee who did nothing wrong?
takeaway: In a serial payment, every bank in the chain takes its cut from the amount.

explain:
A company made its first ever payment to a new beneficiary bank: EUR 18,000 for an urgent order. The MT103 was rejected before it was even read.

Nobody had asked the beneficiary bank to accept messages from the sending bank.

Here is what happened:

→ New beneficiary bank identified, payment prepared
→ MT103 sent over SWIFT
→ Receiving bank system refuses the message
→ Payment never arrives, order delayed
→ Team resends the same MT103, rejected again

The requirement said:
"If we have the BIC, we can send the payment."

So the payment was built, approved and sent with no check that the receiving bank would accept it.

Why?

Before one bank can send an MT103 to another over SWIFT, the receiving bank must set up an RMA, a relationship management authorisation, for that sender. Without an RMA the receiving bank's system will not accept the message. The RMA is therefore a precondition for the payment, not a formality that can be sorted out afterwards.

Authorisation comes before the payment, not after it.

Standing settlement instructions matter the same way. Banks tell each other how to send them funds in each currency through SSIs, exchanged as MT670 and MT671 messages. A sender who does not know the receiver's correspondent must find it out through SWIFT services or by asking the receiver directly, before sending.

BA Takeaway

Check the door is open before you send the payment through it.

Keep these controls separate:

→ RMA in place for the receiving bank
→ Standing settlement instructions on file
→ Pre-send validation for a new beneficiary bank

The real requirement is not "Do we have the BIC?"

It is "What evidence proves the receiving bank will accept our message?"

Have you ever sent a payment to a bank that was never set up to receive it?
takeaway: Authorisation comes before the payment, not after it.

explain:
A payer sent GBP 12,000 to a supplier.
Verification of Payee returned No Match.
The payer carried on, and the money went to the wrong account.

Here is what happened:

→ Payer enters the payee name and account details
→ VoP check returns No Match
→ Payer reviews the warning and continues anyway
→ Payment reaches the wrong payee

The requirement said:
"A No Match stops the payment."

But the build did not stop it. Depending on the bank process, the payer can review and correct the details, or continue knowing the payment may reach the wrong payee.

Why?

A No Match says only that the name does not match the name the payee bank holds. It does not say whether it is fraud or a simple typing error, a trading name, or a joint account held under a different name. The check warns, it does not decide.

No Match is a warning, not a verdict.

BA Takeaway

A name check, a payer decision and a payment outcome are three different things, so keep them separate:

→ VoP result
→ Payer decision to correct or continue
→ Payment destination confirmed

Add a clear warning, a correction path, and a record of the payer choosing to continue.

The real requirement is not "When do we stop the payment?"

It is "What evidence proves the payer understood the risk before continuing?"

Have you seen a No Match warning ignored and the money land in the wrong account?
takeaway: No Match is a warning, not a verdict.
